entry.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut large language model prices by up to 80% over several months amid competitive pressure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI and Anthropic have significantly reduced the prices of their large language models (LLMs) by as much as 80% since June 2026, with multiple price cuts announced for various models including GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5.5. These reductions have occurred alongside new model releases and improvements, with no apparent compromise in output quality. The timeline shows a pattern of competitive responses between the two companies, with price cuts often following each other's announcements. Notably, reductions in cache read costs, which constitute a large portion of token expenditure in agentic coding, have contributed substantially to overall cost decreases. Despite lower prices, aggregate spending on LLM usage has increased due to faster improvements in model capabilities. This pricing trend reflects behavioral economics and competitive dynamics in the AI model market, suggesting external factors beyond simple cost reductions are influencing these aggressive price cuts. The moves aim to attract more users and maintain market share as LLMs become more capable and widely adopted.

entry.title: UC Berkeley math professor stops grading homework due to widespread AI use among students, citing AI's growing capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Richard Borcherds, a UC Berkeley math professor and Fields medalist, has ceased grading homework for correctness after observing that many students use AI tools to achieve top scores. He now grades only on completion, acknowledging this is an imperfect system but feeling there is no alternative as AI use becomes unavoidable in coursework. Borcherds expressed uncertainty about the future of mathematics as a career, noting that AI advancements, including recent claims of AI solving complex math problems, may soon surpass human mathematicians. The university's Academic Senate recommends faculty include AI use policies in syllabi, but enforcement varies, and current AI detection tools have proven inadequate for standard campus-wide use.

entry.title: Cerebras deploys multi-trillion parameter AI models using multiple WSE-3T wafers with 44 GB on-chip memory each [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Cerebras explains how it deploys large AI models with trillions of parameters on its wafer-scale engine chips by splitting models across multiple WSE-3T wafers, each with 44 GB of on-chip memory. Using the open source Kimi K3 model with about 3 trillion parameters as an example, Cerebras details how it fits model layers onto wafers, connects wafers in a pipeline, and manages concurrent requests to achieve high throughput. The approach involves placing dense and linear-attention layers on wafers according to their memory needs, with dense layers requiring additional key-value cache space. The wafers communicate activations via low-latency RDMA over Ethernet, allowing model weights to remain on-chip. Requests are processed in a pipeline fashion, with multiple requests handled simultaneously across different wafers to maximize efficiency and throughput.

entry.title: Nvidia partners with German firm to explore converting decommissioned nuclear plants into AI data centers using existing infrastructure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Nvidia has entered a preliminary partnership with German energy company PreussenElektra GmbH to assess the feasibility of repurposing shut-down nuclear power plant sites in Germany into high-performance AI data centers. The project focuses on leveraging existing power, water, and industrial infrastructure at these sites without using nuclear power to run the data centers. The exploration will evaluate the sites' energy grid connections, land availability, and infrastructure to meet the operational needs of AI data centers, aiming to reduce costs and development time compared to building new facilities from scratch. Germany permanently shut down its last nuclear plants in April 2023, and PreussenElektra is responsible for dismantling several sites that may be considered for this initiative, which remains in an experimental phase with no finalized investments or construction plans.

entry.title: Report says AI industry's heavy borrowing and circular financing risk triggering a financial crash beyond tech sector
entry.summary: A report from the Open Markets Institute warns that the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure spending by major U.S. tech companies has led to heavy borrowing and speculative debt practices reminiscent of the subprime bubble. This debt is being repackaged and sold to institutional investors, raising concerns about financial contagion beyond the technology sector. The report highlights that current regulatory rollbacks may worsen these risks and calls for urgent policy action to increase transparency, protect retirement savings, and strengthen financial system resilience. The report does not predict an inevitable crisis but stresses that the conditions for one are present and that timely intervention is critical to prevent economic instability.

entry.title: Bend launches a fast programming language that enforces AI code correctness through formal proofs and law-based rules [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Bend is a new programming language designed to improve AI system reliability by requiring mathematical proofs that enforce application rules, preventing bugs and unintended behavior. It compiles to fast executables comparable to C and CUDA performance and supports parallel execution across thousands of GPU cores. Bend introduces a LAWS.bend file where developers declare rules their applications must follow, and the compiler demands proofs that these laws hold whenever code changes. This approach blocks AI-generated mistakes by making it mathematically impossible to violate declared laws, enabling more trustworthy AI-driven software development. The language is currently optimized for backend use on Linux and macOS systems.

entry.title: DuckDB developers outline eight security risks and mitigation strategies for running DuckDB servers in production environments
entry.summary: The article examines security challenges when deploying DuckDB as a shared server, where SQL users are not the operating system user running the process. It identifies eight classes of exposure, including credential leakage through environment variables, command lines, and persistent secrets, and the risk of unauthorized filesystem access via SQL queries. The authors provide concrete examples and recommend best practices to prevent unauthorized data access and maintain data integrity. Key mitigations include isolating secrets in owner-only directories deleted after use, disabling persistent secrets by restricting secret directories, and controlling filesystem access by limiting SQL query capabilities. The article also describes how the Quack on Demand system implements these protections by default, including a gateway that validates SQL statements before execution to enforce security policies. These measures aim to adapt DuckDB's default assumptions-appropriate for single-user laptop use-to the multi-user server context, reducing the risk of unintended data exposure and ensuring safer production deployments.

The app runs locally on macOS 14 or later, overlays effects on the desktop without saving or sending data, and supports multiple glitch sound options. It integrates with AI agents like Codex via a command-line interface and a local server to manage alert signals and approval workflows. The project is open source under the MIT license and includes tools for customization and packaging.

entry.title: Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI advises against designating specific mathematicians for early AI output releases due to risks of delayed access, bias, and reduced community agency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence has recommended that AI labs avoid designating particular mathematicians to receive and interpret AI-generated mathematical results before public release. They argue this practice can delay or restrict access for other researchers, introduce bias based on the labs' selection, and limit the mathematical community's agency in understanding and developing the results. The group acknowledges the valuable work done by designated mathematicians in past releases but highlights concerns including unequal access, potential conflicts of interest, and the risk that designated mathematicians' reputations may be used to shield AI companies from criticism. They suggest that human understanding of AI-generated mathematics can develop organically when outputs are released publicly, supported by community-led reading groups and workshops. The group recommends AI labs follow established pathways for releasing AI-generated mathematical content that emphasize transparency, community standards, and broad accessibility.

The developer highlights concerns about environmental impact, cultural appropriation, security risks, and privacy violations associated with AI companies. The post reflects frustration over the shrinking pool of non-AI-assisted programs and the challenge of avoiding AI in software, especially as AI involvement extends even to operating system components.

The AI-generated footage, created in collaboration with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker, features Musk-approved casting choices and a British-accented narration. entry.title: OpenAI and Anthropic models solve longstanding mathematical problems including Erdős's conjecture and Navier-Stokes proof, showing new AI capabilities in math [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Recent AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic have solved several longstanding open mathematical problems, such as a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture and a proof of the Navier-Stokes problem. These advances demonstrate AI's growing ability to handle complex mathematical reasoning by leveraging different problem-solving approaches than humans, such as depth-first search and extensive computational effort. The models' success is attributed to their capacity to explore problem spaces differently from human researchers, who typically use breadth-first search constrained by time and effort. AI systems can rapidly test many hypotheses and build on prior knowledge embedded during training, enabling them to tackle problems previously considered intractable or requiring years of human effort. This shift may influence future directions in mathematical research and AI applications in scientific discovery.

entry.title: Limitbreak launches Claude Code proxy to switch between multiple Claude accounts automatically when usage limits are reached, preserving session history [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Limitbreak has developed Claude Code, a local proxy that enables users to switch seamlessly between multiple Claude AI accounts when an account hits its usage limit, without restarting the session or losing conversation history. The proxy intercepts API requests and reroutes them to the next available account, ensuring uninterrupted service. The tool runs as a lightweight Go binary on macOS or Linux and manages account tokens securely, refreshing them as needed. It supports multiple accounts signed in through Claude Code's own browser sign-in process and logs account switches for transparency. Users should be aware that spreading load across accounts may conflict with Anthropic's terms of service, and the tool is not affiliated with Anthropic.

entry.title: A Neocloud's Gathering Storm [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Welcome, Weekenders! Whenever I'm the slightest bit ill, I take to my bed and mope. If it goes more than a day or so, I assume the worst-that the end is nigh. I can't honestly remember the last time I felt unwell for more than a couple days, but I imagine such a scenario would probably find me consulting ChatGPT about burial shrouds. So I'd like to extend a smidgen of sympathy to CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator. Surely, he's been feeling poorly for nearly two weeks! In the last 12 days, CoreWeave's stock has been nearly halved. A confluence of factors has contributed to the rampant decline, as my colleague Dakin Campbell explained. In short, investors are worried about how rising interest rates will affect CoreWeave's ability to raise debt, which it needs to fund its business of selling cloud computing services. They're also concerned about whether CoreWeave can handle the costs of the mound of debt it already has. Last week, fresh data on U.S. inflation fueled interest rate concerns: Inflation jumped in September, increasing the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates-making all debt more expensive. Even though there was no new inflation data this week, CoreWeave shares continued to fall-from around $60 on Monday to roughly $54 on Friday. Not even Nvidia's all-powerful CEO, Jensen Huang, was able to stanch the bleeding when he tried to sound a note of confidence for CoreWeave on Thursday, saying the demand for companies like CoreWeave-neoclouds-is "off the charts." The stock nerds over at Barron's tried to argue that Wednesday's earnings report from SpaceX is actually a good sign for CoreWeave. Those numbers showed surging demand for SpaceX's nascent business of selling its excess AI compute, but I'm not sure whether that necessarily bodes well for the company. Yes, an indicator of demand for compute could be interpreted as a welcome data point for CoreWeave, a compute seller. But SpaceX's compute business increasingly seems like a real competitor to CoreWeave and other neoclouds, and as the much, much better established company, SpaceX has the resources to fund expansion of its compute-selling efforts without acquiring hazardous amounts of debt. And investors are a great deal less likely to sink its stock price over interest rate jitters. More news from Wednesday highlighted the industry's appetite for compute. Meta Platforms said it will create a new share class in January-essentially a two-for-one stock split-that will allow it to reach for more capital to spend on AI. It's also partly a maneuver that would help CEO Mark Zuckerberg pay off California's billionaire tax if the levy is approved next month. Meta's board justified helping Zuck pay his taxes by saying that the CEO had threatened to pick up sticks and leave California-and that it was essential to have him in the office as much as possible. (I had to laugh. Just a couple years ago, Zuckerberg was telling us the metaverse would arrive soon, and we'd all be living as digital stick things. Such was the potential of the metaverse that Zuckerberg renamed his entire company for it. Well, guess not!) More capital at Meta might be good for CoreWeave. Meta is a CoreWeave customer-to the tune of $35 billion. There's no guarantee, of course, that Meta will take a newfound gusher of capital and go back to CoreWeave again. Recently, Meta has been building its own data centers and readying production of its custom AI chips. It has also considered selling compute. Investors looked on wearily at Meta's stock split/potential Zuck gift, with the company's shares dropping nearly 9% on Thursday. In fact, Meta's moves unnerved the entire market yet again over how much this whole AI thing will cost. The Nasdaq sank 2.6% on Thursday. CoreWeave shares fell 10%, while declines also hit Nebius (down 7.2%) and IREN (8.3%), the two other publicly traded neoclouds. And everything kept falling on Friday. Are all the stock moves based on buttoned-up rationality? No. But like the common cold that I'm always certain will put me six feet under, worry on Wall Street is contagious.-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) The Information's Must-Read Stories Ramp Investors Went Nuclear Against Airwallex After Doomed Deal Hackers Used Claude and Grok to Automate Attacks on Banks How CoreWeave's Debt Binge Brought a Moment of Reckoning Listening: "Bear Brook: A Private Matter" Back in 2017, NHPR, a little public radio station in New Hampshire, found itself with a hit national podcast, "Bear Brook," about cold-case murders-four bodies in two barrels stashed in Bear Brook State Park-and the genetic testing involved in investigating the crimes. Reporter Jason Moon followed up with a second season about a different crime in 2023 and now returns with a third season about another weird happening: the disappearance of 76-year-old Jay Hickey, a local Christmas tree farmer. (Moon likens the setting to a Hallmark movie-frankly, it gave me distinct "Twin Peaks" vibes.) After Hickey vanished one autumn, it was months before anyone went looking for him. That was strange because he was suffering from dementia, so surely his wife, Pat, would've, uh, noticed he wasn't around, right? Obviously she offed him, right? Perhaps, but she clearly was suffering from something herself. It's the type of tale that could be glossed over with schlock, sordid storytelling. That's definitely not Moon's approach.-Abram Brown Reading: "Kobuk the Destroyer" by Alex Davies Just in the past 12 hours, I've dodged a number of possible catastrophes: I was not singed by my hair dryer, crushed by my office's elevator doors or left unproductive by a bunch of buttons tumbling out of my keyboard. I owe my good fortune to the rigorous science of product testing, a gorpy-seeming topic made into enlightening, witty entertainment in "Kobuk the Destroyer" by Alex Davies, a former Wired magazine editor. It is an ode to the nerd geniuses who devise those tests, but it can also feel like a drop directly onto the factory floor of Looney Tunes' Acme Corporation, presenting a sharp critique of how often executives cut corners and ignore blatant problems as they pursue commercialization. Without the centurylong expansion of product testing, we'd all be left in the same position as Wile E. Coyote, with faulty, rocket-powered roller skates attached to our feet. The titular Kobuk, a grizzly bear, may be one of the most prolific practitioners of the field-having lived out the last several decades at a Montana wildlife sanctuary that partners with a government agency to certify various products as bear proof. Kobuk has the great joy of tearing apart coolers, trash cans, composters, and many other items, and gets rewarded with fish, peanut butter, honey, and dog biscuits for his efforts: Whatever survives Kobuk's assault receives the certification. Through his efforts, the general public can buy coolers that actually do keep out other Kobuks. Theoretically, that prevents his shaggy-haired brethren from learning to filch food or hang around humans, habits that can get a bear relocated or euthanized. Kobuk has pawed his way onto a noble path initially blazed in the 1920s by Underwriters Laboratories, a Chicago-based business that pioneered the art of product testing-with engineers who assessed the durability of safes by subjecting them to thousand-degree heat, 30-foot drops and kerosene-fueled explosions. Davies keeps up a brisk pace as he winds through the many testing approaches adopted by various industries in the following years, including the NASA wind tunnel used to develop the Curiosity Mars lander and the oval-shaped gelatin sacks that engineers fired into airplane engines to avoid needing to kill thousands and thousands of live birds. As many of you might surely agree, determining the safety of one group of products in particular remains decidedly challenging: ahem, AI! Much of the alignment training and red teaming that goes into AI development comes away with vague conclusions, Davies writes: We simply don't understand enough about what we've created, and AI often operates much more unpredictably than, say, a refrigerator door or an airbag. Trying to understand why an AI behaved safely in one setting but dangerously in another is "like trying to understand why your dog growls at people carrying shopping bags but not people carrying suitcases."-A.B. Watching: "Carrie" Stephen King's cabinet of terrors is a well-stocked place, cluttered with weird evils, many with complex, lengthy backstories. The It of "It," you may recall, is not actually an evil clown-it's an ageless, alien ball of light. "The Langoliers" is a time-travel story...about piranha-like, interdimensional critters that literally eat time. I could try to also get into the motivations of Randall Flagg in "The Stand," but unlike King, I don't have 823 pages to do that here. The knottier of King's novels defy easy screen adaptations. Other retellings of King stories fail on the screen largely because they suffer in comparison to finer, earlier movie adaptations, to say nothing of their misappropriation of King's material. On Amazon, there's an excellent new restructuring of King's "Carrie," his first bestseller and, of course, the source for a much-loved film by director Brian De Palma, which put both De Palma and King on the map. There's a simplicity and universal resonance to King's story of tortured, telekinetic high schooler Carrie White that makes it highly moldable: Teenagers have been terrifying ever since there have been teenagers, both to themselves and to those around them. Amazon's "Carrie" was helmed by Mike Flanagan, who has a string of spooky series on Netflix ("The Fall of the House of Usher," "The Haunting of Hill House") and did the 2019 movie adaptation of King's "Doctor Sleep." Flanagan adeptly positions his "Carrie" in the modern day. The infamous shower scene, for example, does not really end when Carrie (newcomer Summer Howell) is escorted away by kindhearted PE teacher Miss Desjardin (Amber Midthunder). Her bullying classmates captured the entire thing on their cellphones, and their torment of her continues via an anonymous Instagram account. Later, her mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan), a religious nut who also favors QAnon-like conspiracy theories, seizes the internet as a means for her own ferocious manipulations. With the benefit of an eight-episode run, Flanagan gets the opportunity to give greater depth to the Whites and the people around them, including Carrie's chief bully, Christine (Alison Thornton), and classmate Sue (Siena Agudong), who befriends Carrie in this version. Granted, it might seem like Flanagan is trying to stretch the material as thin as a funeral crepe. He doesn't, aided by roundly top-notch performances.-A.B.

entry.title: VC Firms Tap LP Pools, Warehouse Loans for Speedy AI Cash [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: When Reflection AI set out to raise $2.5 billion early this year, one of its existing venture backers, B Capital, was eager to invest again in the startup, which has emerged as the most high-profile U.S. maker of open-source AI models. But Reflection's valuation had more than tripled in just six months, forcing investors to write big checks for a sizable stake. Such a check would have been too big for B Capital's main venture fund, a $500 million vehicle raised in July. To come up with the cash, the company turned to a different source of capital: a pool of money apart from its regular fund, designed to give limited partners-the pension funds, endowments and wealthy individuals that back VC firms-more direct access to hot startups like Reflection at reduced fees.

entry.title: Why Blackstone Thinks AI Bottlenecks Could Work in its Favor [ * ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Greetings! On their earnings calls earlier in the week, Meta Platforms and SpaceX delivered the same underlying message to investors: demand for AI is running ahead of the supply of AI compute. On Thursday, another important player in the AI ecosystem-Blackstone, the alternative asset management giant-repeated a version of that refrain. On its own earnings call, the firm, a major investor at the center of the AI data center boom, faced pointed questions from analysts about rising financing costs and mounting investor concerns over the sustainability of the buildout. Its executives argued that the very factors threatening the AI industry's expansion could actually work in Blackstone's favor. CEO Steve Schwarzman noted that constraints on power availability and growing public opposition to new data centers are making it harder to bring new capacity online, potentially making existing facilities more valuable. Blackstone President Jon Gray also suggested the firm could seek higher returns on projects where it hasn't signed leases yet in order to offset rising borrowing costs. Blackstone's third-quarter results offered some support for that argument: Its infrastructure investments were buoyed by what executives called "extraordinary" data center leasing momentum, significantly outperforming its broader private equity and real estate holdings. "Despite all the negative things you're reading about AI today, when we look across our business, this continues to be the area where we're driving the highest returns," Gray said during the call. But it's hard to ignore the fact that the financing concerns and roadblocks threatening the broader AI infrastructure buildout are also hitting closer to home for Blackstone. Fears about rising financing costs have sent CoreWeave's stock and bond prices plunging-the neocloud's shares closed down another 10% Thursday after sliding last week-while Australian AI cloud provider Firmus abruptly pulled its initial public offering earlier this month. Blackstone has provided billions in loans to CoreWeave and has both invested in and lent money to Firmus. Blackstone has also been pressing ahead with brand-new AI ventures. In May, the firm announced an initial $5 billion equity commitment to a joint venture with Google to create a new cloud company that will use Google's TPU chips, with plans to bring 500 megawatts of capacity online by next year. The venture could need as much as $25 billion in total investment, including some borrowed money, and it has reportedly encountered delays at potential data center sites. Blackstone, for its part, says that broader anxiety about AI hasn't undermined its ability to raise fresh cash for making its own investments. "We're continuing to be able to raise capital. Obviously investors are asking the same question around AI, but what we continue to see is demand and usage of the AI going up faster than the compute," Gray said. While Blackstone says it wants to continue going big in AI, it can only finance a tiny portion of the industry's broader infrastructure buildout itself. The trillions of dollars of financing needed for chips and data centers in the coming years requires raising money from a far broader pool of investors. Blackstone itself has said it's not clear where all the money will come from. Jas Khaira, the head of the team leading Blackstone's push into AI investment, said late last month that the firm is still trying to determine which investors across the public debt and private credit markets will be able to provide the funding needed to sustain the buildout. "We have not mapped out who's going to buy all the debt. We have some hypotheses, but the honest answer is we don't know where all of it will come from," he said at The Information's AI Agenda event in San Francisco. Data Center Headwinds Despite Blackstone's overall positive note on AI demand, we got fresh evidence Thursday afternoon of the uncertainty in the IPO market for companies in the data center business. Phoebe Liu and Valida Pau had a scoop that SB Energy, a company controlled by SoftBank Group that is developing an OpenAI data center in Ohio, is discussing a plan to put off its IPO until December or earlier next year. Previously, SB Energy was aiming to go public in September. The best hope for an SB Energy IPO is that the supply of AI compute gets so tight that investors start warming back up to data centers.-Nick Wingfield In Other News Meta Platforms' stock fell 7% as investor enthusiasm over its third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday gave way to concerns about the probability that it will need to issue new equity to pay for its AI spending. Andreessen Horowitz renamed its flagship blockchain fund a16z Frontier, dropping "crypto" from its name (The Information's earlier scoop on the change is here). Google partnered with energy company Voltus to pay homes and businesses to use less electricity during periods of peak demand. entry.title: Salesforce Customers Brace For New Fees to Use Claude in Its Apps [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Salesforce is leading the software industry's attempt to collect fees from businesses that use Claude and other external AI tools to automate work in enterprise apps. As soon as next month, Salesforce plans to require companies to register outside AI agents, a step toward charging them each time those agents update or analyze data stored in Salesforce. The fees let Salesforce earn money from customers who use such AI instead of paying for Salesforce's built-in AI products. The Salesforce tollgate has implications for the rest of the industry, which is coming to terms with the idea that so-called AI agents may be able to use software firms' apps more efficiently than humans do, meaning their seat-based or per-user pricing model might not have staying power. The question is whether the new AI tollgates-which Atlassian, Workday, ServiceNow and Datadog are also erecting to various extents-and other pricing shifts will more than make up for an eventual decline in per-seat subscription revenues. The vast majority of workers haven't yet outsourced such work to AI, of course, and companies like Salesforce are trying to get more revenue from them as well. They charge fees based on how much they use the apps' built-in AI tools and are also experimenting with outcome-based pricing, meaning customers only pay when such tools actually complete a task successfully or help the customers make more money. For now, Salesforce and some other software firms developing tollgates for customers' AI agents haven't started charging the tolls. They're letting customers experiment for free with the technology a little while longer. (The customers still have to pay providers such as Anthropic to use the AI agents in the first place.) Starting around November, according to the company's website, Salesforce will require customers to register any externally-made AI agents if they plan to use them to take actions on their behalf in Salesforce apps. Each action an agent takes in Salesforce counts as a billable "interaction," according to the company. The move has lifted investor confidence in Salesforce recently. Salesforce describes the registration requirement as a security measure because the company gives each agent its own identity and narrower data-access permissions, compared to humans. It isn't clear how Salesforce will clamp down on customers using their own AI agents, such as OpenClaw-powered ones that run on a person's computer and can access any app that runs on it. (Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.) Salesforce hasn't announced prices tied to such agent usage, but customers could eventually end up paying a lot more money than they do now, given how many of them are already using their own AI on top of Salesforce apps and bypassing Salesforce's own built-in AI tools, according to software consultants and chief information officers. Nick Hamm, a software consultant, said that most of the 150 enterprises he works with are currently using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to automate work inside Salesforce apps, for free. But they're reconsidering that usage in anticipation of the upcoming fees. If the fees are too high, the customers may move their business data outside of Salesforce's apps so they can use AI to analyze the data without paying an extra cost, he said. New customers will have a three month grace period after the new pricing is announced to register their AI agents, and the pricing won't affect existing customers until their contracts are renewed. In addition to the billable "interactions," customers have the option to buy unlimited agent usage by purchasing a "headless license," a Salesforce account executive told Hamm in a LinkedIn message viewed by The Information. Some customers such as Lumen, a fiber-optic network provider to enterprises and data centers, say they are waiting to test Salesforce's new connectors until pricing is disclosed. So far, Lumen has leaned on Salesforce's built-in AI. A longtime customer of Salesforce's customer relationship management software, Lumen made a "major" investment in using Salesforce's AI sales agents in the last 12 months, according to CIO Jim Fowler. The sales agents help with tasks such as collecting customer information and generating sales quotes for the customers to buy fiber connections between data centers, saving Lumen's human salespeople considerable time, he said. So far, Fowler said, Salesforce has been "super flexible" about letting Lumen use existing subscription fees to also cover its use of built-in AI features such as the sales agents. Early customer reactions to the pricing announcement will likely determine how flexible Salesforce is with customers that start renewing their contracts after November. If its past AI pricing efforts are any guide, Salesforce could easily switch things up depending on the feedback, or any blowback, it receives.
